chunks: Design a sample and hold circuit. The question: Design a sample and hold circuit.
Designing a sample-and-hold means choosing the parts of a switch, a capacitor and two amplifiers so that it grabs an input quickly and holds it accurately.
You start from the requirements, then pick the capacitor and the switch size with numbers. The main trade-off is that a bigger capacitor holds better but takes longer to charge.
Think of filling a cup from a tap and then carrying it across the room. You want the cup to fill fast, so you want a wide tap and a small cup.
You want it to stay full on the way, so you want a big cup with no leaks. Those two wishes pull in opposite directions, and the design is the compromise.
The capacitor is the cup, and the switch is the tap.
A1 buffers the source so the switch sees a low impedance, M1 (clocked by φ) is the sampling switch, C H holds the voltage and A2 isolates C H from the ADC.
In a real design M1 would be a transmission gate or bootstrapped, with a dummy switch for charge cancellation.
Hold capacitor: ("What is sample and hold?") : the capacitor that stores the sampled voltage. Time constant: switch resistance times capacitance.
It sets how fast the capacitor charges. Settling: the capacitor getting close enough to the input voltage. About 9 time constants gets within half a step of a 12-bit ADC.
Charge injection: a small jolt of charge the switch pushes into the capacitor when it opens. Droop: ("How a sample is held steady"): the slow sag of the held voltage from leakage.
Say the design is 12-bit for a 0 to 3. 3 volts input, sampled at 1 million samples per second. Each sample gets 1 microseconds: 0. 4 microseconds to track and 0.
6 microseconds to hold. Pick a 10 picofarads hold capacitor. Settling needs about 9 time constants in 0. 4 microseconds, so the time constant must be under about 44 nanoseconds.
Then R = 44 nanoseconds / 10 picofarads = 4. 4 kilohms at most, so a 500 ohms to 1 kilohms switch leaves plenty of margin. That is the whole idea.
"I'd start from the spec: 12 bits, 3. 3 volts, 100 kilohertz, 1 MS/s. The circuit is an input buffer, an NMOS or transmission-gate switch, a hold capacitor and an output buffer.
I'd pick 10 picofarads so kT/C noise is about 20 µV and droop is tiny, then size the switch so settling to half an LSB, nine time constants, fits in the track window: under 4 kilohms at 0.
4 microseconds. I'd use a dummy switch to cancel charge injection and a bootstrapped gate to keep Ron constant, and keep clock jitter under about 0. 3 nanoseconds."
